claims.claim: The SQL JOIN clause combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column between them.
Queries that access multiple tables at once are called join queries; they combine rows from one table with rows from a second table, with an expression specifying which rows are to be paired.
Joins retrieve data from multiple tables based on logical relationships between them and combine data from two or more tables into a single result set.
INNER JOIN returns only rows that have matching values in both tables; the INNER keyword is optional, so JOIN alone is an inner join.
LEFT (OUTER) JOIN returns all rows from the left table and only the matched rows from the right table.
With an ON clause, the join expression is evaluated for each row of the full pairing, and only the rows for which it is true are included in the result.
A typical join condition specifies a foreign key from one table and its associated key in the other table.

The explicit JOIN/ON syntax was introduced in SQL-92, and the older implicit join written in WHERE produces identical results for inner joins, which is why the explicit form is recommended for clarity.
A join with no ON or USING clause produces the cartesian product of the two tables.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether 'most common' is a fair label for INNER JOIN.
positions: Every surveyed reference presents plain JOIN as an inner join (INNER is optional) and lists it first among join types.
No surveyed source publishes a usage statistic.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson says INNER JOIN is the default (the keyword is optional, per W3Schools and Microsoft syntax) and the type you will meet most often; no statistical frequency claim is made.

conflictingEvidence.issue: ON condition versus WHERE for pairing rows.
positions: Pre-SQL-92 syntax lists the tables in FROM and writes the matching condition in WHERE.
Modern syntax introduces the join condition with its own keyword ON.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: PostgreSQL documents that the results are identical for the classic inner join and recommends the explicit JOIN/ON form for clarity; the lesson follows that recommendation.
